money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The local currency is the Djibouti Franc (DJF). Travellers cheques can be exchanged at major banks. Djibouti has a cash-based economy. Credit cards aren't widely accepted. USD can be changed at major hotels and some banks. There are a limited number of ATMs, but they often don't work. Ask your bank if your card will work in Djibouti.

laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe and include long jail sentences and heavy fines. The narcotic khat is legal in Djibouti, but illegal in many other countries.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Illegal activities in Djibouti include: hunting being drunk in public photographing military personnel It's illegal to photograph military facilities and public infrastructure, such as government buildings, ports, airports and bridges If you take photos near prohibited places, you may: have your equipment confiscated be arrested If in doubt, ask for advice from local authorities.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Same-sex relationships are not illegal in Djibouti but authorities may prosecute same-sex couples displaying affection in public. - Advice for LGBTQIA+ travellers
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ information

laws.rule: The Islamic holy month of Ramadan is observed in Djibouti. Respect religious and cultural customs and laws at this time. During Ramadan, avoid eating, drinking and smoking in public during the day. If you're not fasting, avoid these activities around people who are. Seek local advice to avoid offence. Airline schedules can be affected during the month of Ramadan. Check flight schedules with your travel provider. Explore our Ramadan page to learn more, including dates for Ramadan.
laws.heading: Cultural dates

laws.rule: To drive in Djibouti, you need both: a valid Australian driver’s licence (digital driver's licences may not be accepted) a valid International Driving Permit (IDP) You must get your IDP before leaving Australia.
laws.heading: Driving permit

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: During Ramadan do not eat, drink, smoke or chew gum in public in daytime, play loud music, dance or swear in public, and follow local dress codes. Drinking is allowed but drunken behaviour can bring a 2-year sentence. Do not photograph ports, public buildings, airports, military sites or bridges. Cards are not widely accepted; carry cash.

events.what: Ramadan, the Muslim month of fasting, expected about 8 February to 8 or 9 March 2027 (set by moon sighting)
events.effect: Many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. Some cafés and restaurants close by day and business hours shorten; eating, drinking or smoking in public in daylight can cause offence. Evenings are busy after the fast is broken.

events.what: Eid al-Fitr, the end of Ramadan, expected 9 March 2027 (set by moon sighting; may fall a day later)
events.effect: Public holiday: offices and many shops close; buses, flights and hotels busy as people travel to family.

events.what: Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice, expected 16 May 2027 (set by moon sighting; may fall a day later)
events.effect: Public holiday: offices and many shops close; buses, flights and hotels busy as people travel to family.

events.what: Islamic New Year (Awal Muharram), expected about 6 June 2027 (set by moon sighting)

events.effect: Public holiday: offices and banks close; official ceremonies and parades, with some road closures.

events.what: Mawlid, the Prophet's Birthday, expected about 14 to 15 August 2027 (set by moon sighting)
events.effect: Public holiday: offices close; religious gatherings and processions in some towns.
